title: 93 Evaluating the relationship between anogenital distance and fertility in beef cattle females
content:
Abstract
It has been previously demonstrated that an inverse correlation exists between anogenital distance (AGD) and measurements of fertility in dairy cows and heifers. Such fertility differences observed based on AGD could allow the use of AGD as a tool for selection of beef replacement heifers and aid in reproductive efficiency of cow-calf operations. The objective of the present study was to explore relationships between anogenital distance and pregnancy outcomes to timed-artificial insemination (TAI) in commercial beef cows and heifers. The AGD was assessed in commercial Bos indicus (n=658) and Bos taurus (n=1419) beef cows (n=653) and heifers (n=1424) from 8 different locations during the years of 2023 and 2024 in U.S. (n=1399) and Brazil (n=678). All females were exposed to controlled internal drug release (CIDR)-based estrous synchronization protocols and exposed to TAI. Conception rates to TAI were assessed approximately 45 days post-TAI through transrectal ultrasonography. Measurements of AGD were assessed by utilizing a digital caliper at either CIDR insertion, CIDR withdrawal, TAI, or pregnancy diagnosis, depending on location and defined as the distance from the middle of the anus to the base of the clitoris. There were significant effects of parity (P< 0.0001), location (P< 0.0001) and day of measurement (P< 0.05) for AGD measurements. Additionally, there were no differences for TAI pregnancy outcome based on parity (P=0.82), day of measurement (P=0.85), or subspecies*AGD (P=0.66). No linearPearson correlations were found between AGD and pregnancy to TAI (r=-0.001; P=0.503); however, there was an effect of location (P< 0.0001) and AGD (P=0.03) on pregnancy outcome to TAI; pregnant=99.14 mm (n=1078); open=100.55 mm (n=999). We conclude that beef females with shorter AGD have greater pregnancy success when exposed to TAI programs. However, the small numerical difference of 1.4mm observed between open and pregnant females make the use of AGD as a selection tool for replacement heifers difficult.
